title: Quizartinib and omacetaxine mepesuccinate combination therapy in FLT3-ITD AML: a phase II trial

paper_content.abstract: FLT3-ITD inhibitors are approved for acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) treatment but relapse is common. In this study, the combined inhibition of FLT3-ITD signal and protein translation by QUIZartinib and Omacetaxine Mepesuccinate (QUIZOM) synergistically suppressed the most critical FLT3-ITD survival signals including mitochondrial respiration and proteostasis, which induced apoptosis and pro-inflammatory response. In a Phase 2 trial (NCT03135054) involving 40 chemo-refractory/unfit FLT3-ITD AML patients, QUIZOM achieved a composite complete remission (CRc) of 83%, a median leukemia-free survival (LFS) of 10 months (Range: 0.7-68.2 months) and a median overall survival (OS) of 12.9 months (Range: 1.8-69.2 months). 13/33 (39%) received allogeneic HSCT after a median of 143 days (Range: 53-367 days). Higher CRc rates were observed in patients with NPM1 mutations, DNMT3A mutations, and wild-type WT1. Single-cell RNA-sequencing of QUIZOM cohort revealed positive correlation between pro-inflammatory response in blasts, CD8+T activation and clinical responsiveness. Further, we identified a leukaemic stem cell (LSC) subpopulation with activated JNK/JUN/HSPA1B axis via PLD1-driven phosphatidylcholine metabolism, which promoted proteostasis and drove QUIZOM resistance. PLD1-inhibitor remodeled phospholipid metabolism, induced ferroptosis and restored QUIZOM response in LSC. Our findings provided the therapeutic and resistant mechanisms of QUIZOM and paved the way for targeted interventions in this AML subtype.
paper_content.introduction:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is characterized by an abnormal increase in myeloblasts in blood and bone marrow (BM) due to differentiation blockade and increased proliferation. FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3-internal tandem duplication (FLT3-ITD) is one of the most common mutations in AML, accounting for up to 30% of cases. In-frame insertion of the duplicated sequence leads to constitutive activation of FLT3, which drives cellular proliferation via activation of oncogenic pathways viz. PI3K, STAT5 and RAS.1 AML carrying FLT3-ITD is associated with a higher risk of relapse and inferior prognosis.2

FLT3 inhibitors are now available for clinical use at relapse. 3-6 Despite an improved outcome compared with standard of care (SOC), the clinical benefit of FLT3 inhibitor monotherapy, notably gilteritinib and quizartinib, is characteristically transient and relapse is uniform unless allogeneic HSCT can be timely arranged.7,8 There is an unmet clinical need to identify the oncogenic vulnerabilities in FLT3-ITD AML and develop mechanism-driven therapeutic strategies at relapse so that more patients can be bridged to HSCT.

In this study, we examined the oncogenic vulnerabilities in FLT3-ITD AML and showed that they were specifically sensitive to perturbation of FLT3-ITD signal and protein translation, which was proven both in the laboratory and in a Phase II clinical trial. Combination treatment with Quizartinib and Omacetaxine mepesuccinate (referred herein QUIZOM) disrupted proteostasis, leading to apoptosis, DNA damage, and activation of inflammatory pathways. Clinical resistance to QUIZOM is associated with increased activity of PLD1-driven phosphatidylcholine metabolism which promoted proteostasis in a leukaemic stem cell (LSC) subpopulation. Inhibition of PLD1 mitigated the resistance in LSC population by remodelling metabolism and inducing ferroptosis. The mechanisms underlying the therapeutic efficacy and subsequent relapses have become important leads for further research that may further improve the outcome in this AML subtype.
paper_content.results:
Summary of patient recruitment, primary and secondary outcomes in QUIZOM clinical trial
Forty patients, including 35 relapse/refractory (R/R) and 5 newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD AML patients, were recruited and treated with the combination of quizartinib and omacetaxine mepesuccinate (QUIZOM) between November 2017 and September 2020.

The treatment achieved a composite complete remission (CRc) rate of 83% (33/40 patients). For the entire cohort, the median leukemia-free survival (LFS) was 10 months (range: 0.7-68.2 months). Subgroup analysis showed a median LFS of 6.9 months (range: 0.9-15.7 months) in the newly diagnosed group and 10 months (range: 0.7-68.2 months) in the R/R group.

FLT3-ITD AML is vulnerable to the co-inhibition of FLT3-ITD and protein translation
To identify the vulnerability of FLT3-ITD AML that may become target for intervention, we analyzed the DepMap CRISPR-Cas9 knockout database (https://depmap.org/portal/). FLT3-ITD AML dependency involved genes associated with FLT3 signaling, protein translation and respiratory electron transport (Figure 1A, Supplementary Dataset 5 and 6). Functional validation was performed. There was preferential sensitivity of FLT3-ITD AML towards inhibitor of FLT3-ITD (Quizartinib) and protein translation (Omecetaxine Mepesuccinate, OM) (Figure 1B-1C, Supplementary Fig. 1A-1B). Combination treatment (QUIZOM) synergistically reduced protein synthesis and induced apoptosis in human FLT3-ITD AML cell lines (Figure 1D-1F, Supplementary Fig. 1C-1E) and isogenic Ba/F3-FLT3-ITD cell lines (Figure 1G-1I). The synergism was further validated in primary FLT3-ITD AML samples (Figure 1J-1K) and in xenotransplantation model (Figure 1L-1O and Supplementary Fig. 1F), confirming the therapeutic efficacy of QUIZOM in this AML subtype. At the drug doses used, there was no significant toxicity of QUIZOM in animals (Figure 1P).

QUIZOM synergistically remodeled the translatome in FLT3-ITD AML
To study the mechanism underlying the vulnerability to QUIZOM in FLT3-ITD AML, we examined the effects on newly synthesized proteins (NSPs) (see also Supplementary Note 2) (Figure 2A) and identified 5917 NSPs that showed ≥1 unique peptide in all samples (Supplementary Fig. 2A and Supplementary Dataset 7-10). Substantial decrease in NSPs associated with various biological processes, such as protein folding, cell cycle and RNA metabolism, were observed upon drug treatment (Supplementary Fig. 2B-2D). A total of 165 NSPs (Figure 2B) were selected for subsequent analyses based on pre-determined criteria: log2 fold-change <-0.5 (downregulated) and synergistic score >0.5 (non-antagonistic QUIZOM v.s. monotherapy). Among them, MCL1 (a reported OM target)9 and the 2 most downregulated NSPs (HSP70 and UBL3) was selected for validation by Western blot (Figure 2C). Reportedly, the anti-leukaemic effect of OM might be driven by MCL1 downregulation.9 However, forced expression of MCL1 only partially mitigated the QUIZOM-induced apoptosis suggesting that alternative mechanisms might account for QUIZOM-induced cytotoxicity (Figure 2D and Supplementary Fig. 2E). Gene Ontology analysis of the 165 NSPs showed that they were solely enriched with mitochondrial respiration and chaperone-mediated protein folding functions (Supplementary Dataset 11, Figure 2E), suggesting these processes might account for QUIZOM cytotoxicity.

To investigate the molecular events involved in the QUIZOM-induced translatome remodelling, RNA-seq was performed. QUIZOM significantly upregulated 1689 and 1327 genes and downregulated 1160 and 1577 genes in MV4-11 and MOLM-13 respectively (Supplementary Fig. 2F). Pathway analysis and Western blot confirmed the suppression of FLT3-ITD downstream signal, mTOR/S6K/4E-BP1 axis10, that might account for the synergistic inhibition of protein translation by QUIZOM (Supplementary Fig. 2G-2I). In addition, there was negative enrichment of pathways pertaining to mitochondrial metabolism and chaperone-mediated protein folding (Supplementary Fig. 2J) based on GSEA, consistent with the translatome findings.

The observations of DepMap dependency, translatome and transcriptome aforementioned underscored a key therapeutic effect of QUIZOM via perturbation of mitochondrial function. The latter was further investigated. QUIZOM decreased mitochondrial mass and membrane potential in FLT3-ITD AML (Figure 2F-2G). There was ultrastructural evidence of mitochondria rupture (Figure 2H-2I).

Functionally, QUIZOM significantly reduced both glycolysis (glucose uptake and extracellular acidification rate (ECAR)), mitochondrial respiration and ATP level (Supplementary Fig. 2K-2P), underscoring a significant reduction of functional mitochondria. An untargeted metabolomics was performed and principal component analysis (PCA) confirmed a unique spectrum of metabolic remodeling by QUIZOM, which was distinct from those of single drug treatment (Supplementary Fig. 2Q). In particular, QUIZOM significantly reduced glucose, amino acid and nucleotide metabolism which were reported to be essential in supporting the survival of FLT3-ITD AML (Figure 2K).11-13 However, pathway analysis of metabolites with significant changes upon QUIZOM treatment showed that lipid metabolism was not affected indicating the dispensable role of lipid metabolism in mitochondrial respiration in parental FLT3-ITD AML (Supplementary Fig. 2R). Nicotinamide riboside (NR), a precursor of NAD+ cofactor, could ameliorate the growth inhibitory effect of QUIZOM (Figure 2L-M). NR has been shown to promote mitochondrial biogenesis and mitochondrial respiration14,15. In this study, NR alleviated the adverse effects of QUIZOM on mitochondria and ATP level (Figure 2N-Q). Untargeted metabolomics showed that NR induced increase in sugar and glycerophospholipid metabolism in FLT3-ITD AML upon treatment with QUIZOM (Supplementary Fig. 2S and 2T). Similar effects of QUIZOM and NR rescue were seen in primary FLT3-ITD AML samples (Figure 2R-T).

QUIZOM abrogated mitochondrial-assisted protein refolding and led to apoptosis
Potential effects of QUIZOM on chaperone-mediated protein folding were also examined. QUIZOM was shown to reduce the amount of chaperone protein HSP70 (Figure 2C) and induce the formation of protein aggregates in multiple independent assay platforms (Figure 3A-3B, Supplementary Fig. 3A-3C). Pharmacologic inhibition of HSP70 similarly enhanced the formation of protein aggregates (Figure 3C-3D) and induced apoptosis (Figure 3E-3F) in AML cell lines and primary samples. Bortezomib, a proteasomal inhibitor, was reported to generate protein aggregates by blocking the degradation of misfold protein.16 Addition of Bortezomib potentiated the formation of protein aggregates and apoptosis upon HSP70 inhibition, underscoring the significant role of protein aggregates in QUIZOM induced cytotoxicity (Supplementary Fig. 3D-3E). QUIZOM-induced protein aggregates formation was abolished by NR (Figure 3G), whereas further inhibition of metabolic respiration by PKM2 inhibition (Compound 3k) potentiated HSP70 inhibitor-induced apoptosis (Supplementary Fig. 3F), supporting the proposition of mitochondrial collapse promoting PAs-driven apoptosis (Figure 3H). Furthermore, increased protein aggregates was associated with DNA damage (Figure 3I). DNA damage was reduced by NR supplement, suggesting a causal relationship between mitochondrial function, protein aggregates formation and cytotoxicity (Figure 3J). The aforementioned transcriptome analysis revealed activation of p53 which might be triggered by protein aggregates-inducing DNA damage (Supplementary Fig. 3G). In fact, QUIZOM-induced apoptosis was p53-dependent, as demonstrated by its lack of effects in TP53 loss-of-function mutant MV4-11 isogenic line (Figure 3K). The role of HSP70 in QUIZOM-associated cytotoxicity was further examined by forced expression of HSP70 (HSP70-OE) in AML cell lines, which resulted in the reduced formation of protein aggregates and apoptosis upon QUIZOM treatment in vitro (Figure 3L-3M, Supplementary Fig. 3H) and mitigated the survival benefit of QUIZOM in animals engrafted by MV4-11 (Figure 3N).

QUIZOM activated proinflammatory response in FLT3-ITD AML
In addition to apoptosis, RNA-seq data showed the QUIZOM-induced increase in CDKN1A, a decrease in LMNB1 expression (Supplementary Fig. 4A) and a positive enrichment of pathways associated with senescence associated secretary phenotype (SASP) (Figure 4A-B and Supplementary Dataset 12). QUIZOM induced DNA damage, as shown by the increase in γH2AX in FLT3-ITD AML (Figure 3I). Furthermore,mitochontrial rupture led to an increase in the release of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) to cytoplasm (Figure 4C).17 These changes were associated with STING dimerization, 2’3’-cGAMP production and SASP cytokines (Figure 4D-4F and Supplementary Fig. 4B), characteristic of cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) activation. Treatment with cGAS inhibitor (RU.521), HSP70-OE and NR treatment ameliorated the increases in pro-inflammatory cytokines (Figure 4F), supporting the proposition that cGAS-STING activation resulted from the aberration of the aforementioned intracellular signal. Functionally, QUIZOM promoted phagocytosis by macrophages in co-culture with FLT3-ITD AML and the process was also ameliorated by NR or HSP70 overexpression (Figure 4G). Phagocytosis was also ameliorated by the treatment of CCL3 and CSF1 neutralizing antibodies (Figure 4H), suggesting that these cytokines might induce phagocytosis in response to QUIZOM treatment. Importantly, macrophage activation was observed in vivo, as evidenced by their increase in MHC II and CD40 expression (Figure 4I) when NSG mice engrafted by FLT3-ITD AML were treated with QUIZOM.

Phase 2 Clinical trial of QUIZOM in FLT3-ITD AML
The reported synergism and therapeutic mechanisms of QUIZOM laid the foundation of a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating its clinical efficacy and toxicity in FLT3-ITD AML patients. Forty FLT3-ITD AML patients (35 R/R and 5 newly diagnosed) were recruited as previously described. Their clinicopathologic characteristics were shown in Supplementary Dataset 13. The median age was 57.5 years (range: 23-81). Among 35 R/R patients, 11 were primary refractory to “7+3” induction chemotherapy and 14 had two or more prior lines of chemotherapy. Fourteen patients had prior exposure to FLT3 inhibitors, including midostaurin (N=11) and sorafenib (N=3). Seven patients were at post-HSCT relapse (Supplementary Note 2). Median pre-treatment FLT3-ITD allelic ratio was 0.39 (range: 0.03 – 5.72). Targeted gene sequencing of 38 available diagnostic or pre-treatment BM samples showed a median of 3 mutations (range 1-6) (Figure 5A). Similar to other reported cohorts,18 recurrent mutations were seen in DNMT3A (49%), NPM1 (49%), TET2 (17%), RUNX1 (15%), IDH2 (15%) and WT1 (12%). A tyrosine kinase domain (TKD) mutation (p.D835V) of FLT3 was detected in one patient. However, there was no significant change in the top 10 common mutations in the cohort between pretreatment and relapse samples, indicating the genetic changes might not account for the emergence of QUIZOM resistance (Supplementary Fig. 5A) (Supplementary Fig. 5A).

Composite complete remission (CRc) rate was 83% (N=33), including 15% (N=6) CR and 68% (N=27) CRi (Figure 5B). Twenty-nine patients achieved remission after 1 cycle of QUIZOM, and 4 patients after 2 cycles. Median time to response is 23 days (Range: 17-62 days). The median number of cycles received was 3 (range 1-20). The CRc rates were 60% and 86% in upfront treatment and R/R group respectively. Higher CRc rate was observed in patients with mutated NPM1 (95% vs 67%, p=0.038), mutated DNMT3A (95% vs 67%, p=0.038) and wild-type WT1 (91% vs 20%, p=0.002) (Figure 5A) among other clinical parameters (Supplementary Dataset 14). The peripheral blood white cell count decreased within first 48-72 hours of treatment, compatible with induction of apoptosis by QUIZOM (Supplementary Fig. 5B).

Among 33 patients who achieved remission, 13 (39%) received allogeneic HSCT after a median of 143 days (Range: 53-367 days), including 3 from HLA-identical siblings, 4 from haploidentical relatives and 6 from matched unrelated donors (MUD). Twenty-two (63%) patients relapsed, including all who did not receive HSCT (N=19) and 3 patients at 4, 12 and 41 months after HSCT. One patient died of transplant-related mortality and another patient died of infective complication during remission. The median LFS and OS were 10 months (range: 0.7-68.2 months) and 12.9 months (range: 1.8-69.2 months). For patients not bridged to HSCT, the median LFS and OS were 3.3 months and 9.9 months respectively. For patients who were bridged to HSCT, the median LFS and OS were not reached (Figure 5C) at the time of analysis with a median follow up time of 4.7 years. Nine patients remained disease-free at the time of analysis with median LFS at 58.5 months (range: 20.5-68.5 months) and OS at 79 months (range: 22.5-106.3 months). Among 13 relapsed patients with available samples for evaluation, 8 (62%) patients had loss of FLT3-ITD clones at relapse. They had smaller pre-treatment ITD clone size (Supplementary Fig. 5C).

Univariate analysis showed that better overall survival was associated with age ≤ 60 years, achieving CRc, prior FLT3 inhibitor exposure, allogeneic HSCT and wild-type WT1. Superior LFS was associated with age ≤ 60 years and allogeneic HSCT (Supplementary Fig. 5D). Multivariate analysis was not performed due to small cohort size.

There were two early deaths on days 29 and 53 from QUIZOM treatment. They were both non-responding patients and causes of death were pneumonia and pulmonary haemorrhage, and pneumonia respectively, considered to be related to underlying leukaemia progression. Treatment-emergent adverse events were summarised in Supplementary Dataset 15. Grade 3/4 cytopenia and febrile neutropenia were common adverse events. Of note, 20% patients developed bacteraemia (grade 4 sepsis) requiring intravenous antibiotics. Importantly, prolongation of QTc was not observed at the current study dose.

Activation of immune response was associated with clinical QUIZOM response
To delineate the mechanism of QUIZOM responsiveness, single-cell RNA sequencing was performed in 45 samples from 19 unselected patients receiving QUIZOM, from whom serial samples (pre-treatment, remission and relapse/refractory stages) were available (Supplementary Fig. 5E). After integration and unsupervised clustering, 15 major cell populations were identified (Figure 5D-5E). Cell barcode calling was performed to identify AML cells carrying defined mutations (Supplementary Fig. 5F). 19,830 (19,169 with 1 mutation; 661 with ≥2 mutations) out of 439,320 cells were found positive, including mostly haematopoietic stem cell - multipotent progenitor (HSC-MPP), granulocyte-monocyte progenitor (GMP), megakaryocyte progenitor (MkP), and monocyte populations (Figure 5F). A machine learning framework was applied to define the leukaemic and immune populations with high precision and correlation with flow cytometry findings (Supplementary Fig. 5G-5I). The largest leukaemic cell cluster, HSC-MPP, exhibited strong transcriptomic similarity to HSC-MPP cells in previously reported FLT3-ITD samples (Supplementary Fig. 5J).19 QUIZOM treatment resulted in a more drastic reduction of HSC-MPP and significant decreases in GMP and MkP in responders compared to non-responders. Moreover, there were increases in immune populations including CD4-T, CD8-T, Natural Killer T cell (NKT cell), and Natural Killer cell (NK cells), which were not found in non-responders (Figure 5G, Supplementary Fig. 5K).

Single cell transcriptome was analysed to address if the aforementioned activation of immune and inflammatory responses to QUIZOM in the laboratory could be generalized to patients receiving such treatment. Specifically in the responders, QUIZOM induced immune activation, exemplified by the upregulation of interferon responsive genes and IRF2 regulon in the leukaemic HSC-MPP population (Figure 5H, Supplementary Fig. 5L). In addition, QUIZOM resulted in the activation of the T cell Receptor (TCR) pathway in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, and cytotoxicity gene signature in CD8+ T cells at remission (Figure 5I-5K). Gene regulatory network analysis showed a remarkable increase in activity of EOMES and T-bet pertinent to T cell activation and differentiation in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 5L-5M). Furthermore, QUIZOM induced a significant increase in terminally differentiated effector memory CD8+ T cells (TEMRA), decrease in effector memory CD8+ T cells, exhausted CD8+ T cells (TEX) and CD4+ Th17 cells (Figure 5N and Supplementary Fig. 5M). Collectively, the transcriptomic changes in both the leukaemic and immune cell compartments supported the proposition from laboratory studies that the immune system was remodelled by QUIZOM-mediated cytotoxicity on leukaemic blast and such mechanism might correlate with the clinical responsiveness to QUIZOM.

Identification of distinct leukaemic stem cell signature associated with QUIZOM-resistance
Despite the overall satisfactory response to QUIZOM, 4/19 patients did not respond. We further examined the transcriptomic changes after QUIZOM with a view to identify differential changes in the HSC-MPP population of responders compared to non-responders (Supplementary Fig. 6A). Significant and preferential changes were observed in the activity of 29 transcription factors in the HSC-MPP population among responders to QUIZOM (Supplementary Dataset 16), including the down-regulation of HSC genes, such as HOX cluster (Supplementary Fig. 6B).20 Furthermore, the primitive FLT3-ITD-bearing HSC-MPP blast was divided into 7 sub-clusters by unsupervised clustering. Intriguingly, non-responders showed persistence of sub-cluster 0 and 1 (resistant clusters) in the post-treatment samples (Figure 6A-6B, Supplementary Fig. 6C) indicating these clusters might underlie clinical drug resistance. These resistant sub-clusters exhibited up-regulation of gene expression pertinent to leukaemic stem cell, replicative quiescence and lipid metabolism, whereas those associated with protein translation and amino acid metabolism were reduced (Supplementary Fig. 6D-6E). Furthermore, HSC-MPP cells of non-responders on Day 28 of QUIZOM treatment showed a significantly lower pseudotime compared with the responders, attesting to its primitive nature (Figure 6C). We analysed Beat AML public RNA-seq cohort for the impact of LSC signature from this study on overall survival in AML patients. Based on the single cell matrix, AML patients were accorded with high, medium and low LSC fractions using CibersortX. Those with the highest LSC fraction were associated with the worst OS and those with the lowest LSC fraction showed the best OS (Figure 6D). Importantly, QUIZOM resistant LSCs displayed a transcriptome profile distinct from that of chemo-resistant LSC in paediatric AML21, suggesting diverse mechanisms of drug resistance in LSC (Supplementary Fig. 6F).

Putative functions of LSC were examined. LSC preferentially expressed JUN and FOS (key regulators of quiescence, unfolded protein response)22, HSPA1B (encoding HSP70), and genes promoting lipid metabolism such as PLD1, MTMR3, NRR1H2, and SREBF123-25 (Figure 6E-6F and Supplementary Fig. 6G). LSC isolated from primary FLT3-ITD AML samples based on our LSC phenotypic markers CD33+CD44+CD69+ (Figure 6 F) [viz. triple positive (TP) cells] were more replicatively quiescent and less sensitive to QUIZOM than the bulk population (Figure 6G-6I). To validate the functional role of JUN/FOS and PLD1 (phospholipase D1, catalysing the hydrolysis of phosphatidylcholine (PC) to phosphatidate and choline) in the treatment response to QUIZOM, TP of FLT3-ITD primary AML samples were treated by QUIZOM combined with inhibitors to c-Fos/c-Jun (T-5224) and PLD1 inhibitor (VU0155069). T-5224 and VU0155069 synergized with QUIZOM in inducing apoptosis in the TP subpopulation (Figure 6J-K). Combination of PLD1 and QUIZOM resulted in profound suppression of leukaemic engraftment of primary AML (Figure 6L).

To investigate the molecular mechanisms of PLD1 in mediating LSC activity, untargeted metabolomic analysis of TP and bulk population was performed. Glycerophospholipid metabolism was the sole metabolic pathway enriched in TP compared with bulk population (Figure 6M and Supplementary Fig. 6H). In particular, pathway analysis of TP-enriched metabolites reveal the activation of phosphotidylcholine metabolism which was consistent with the upregulation of PLD1 in TP compared to bulk population (Supplementary Fig. 6I). Furthermore, PLD1 inhibition suppressed lipid uptake in TP but not in the bulk population (Figure 6N). PLD1 inhibition remodelled lipid metabolism, leading to increase in ROS and lipid peroxidation (Figure 6O-P). Furthermore, treatment with ferrostatin but not necrostatin mitigated the QUIZOM and PLD1 inhibition-induced cell death, underscoring the induction of ferroptosis by the latter treatment in the TP LSC subpopulation (Figure 6Q). PLD1 overexpression induced lipid uptake (Figure 6R) and ameliorated the QUIZOM-induced apoptosis (Figure 6S), supporting the role of PLD1 in mediating QUIZOM resistance in AML. Supplementation of phosphatidylcholine (PC), the substrate of PLD1, also induced QUIZOM resistance in AML (Supplementary Fig. 6J and 6K). Furthermore, PC significantly reduced QUIZOM-induced formation of protein aggregates (Supplementary Fig. 6L). Mechanistically, PLD1 inhibition preferentially reduced glycerophospholipid metabolism (Supplementary Fig. 6M) and resulted in accumulation of phosphatidylcholines via inhibiting its hydrolysis (Supplementary Fig. 6N). Among the phosphatidylcholines, diacyl-PUFA phosphatidylcholines (PC-PUFA ), a driver of ferroptosis,26 were increased. The observations supported the proposition that PLD1 inhibitor and QUIZOM showed synergizism in suppressing the growth of FLT3-ITD AML via simultaneous induction of apoptosis and ferroptosis.

The putative pathogenetic link between PLD1 expression and the JNK/JUN/HSPA1B axis in LSC population was evaluated (Supplementary Fig. 6O). Inhibition of PLD1 reduced phosphorylation of JNK (Figure 6T). Moreover, inhibition of JNK signaling, FOS/JUN transcriptional activity or PLD1 suppressed the expression HSPA1B (Figure 6U). In primary AML samples, the therapeutic effects of FOS/JUN and PLD1 inhibition on HSPA1B expression and protein aggregates formation were only observed in TP LSC but not the bulk population (Figure 6V-6W).
paper_content.methods:
Detailed descriptions of materials and methods, including cell culture, xenotransplantation studies, translatome and transcriptome analyses, are described in the Supplementary Note 2.

Isotope-metabolic pulse labeling and drug treatments
AML cells were cultured for 24 hours, rinsed with PBS, and cultured in arginine, lysine and methionine depleted RPMI for 30 minutes and modified RPMI containing heavy lysine (13C6-13N2, 0.8 mM Lys8), heavy arginine (13C6-13N4, 0.8 mM Arg10), azidohomoalanine (1 mM AHA) and 10% dialyzed fetal bovine serum. They were treated with quizartinib (2 nM), omacetaxine mepesuccinate (OM, 10 nM), QUIZOM (quizartinib 2 nM + OM 10 nM), or 0.1% DMSO control for 4 hours and lysed. Newly synthesized proteins (NSPs) were isolated by click-chemistry, digested, subjected to tandem mass tag (TMT) multiplexed labelling and deep-scale liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry / mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) (Supplementary Note 2). Translatome data were quantified using Proteome Discoverer and MSstatsTMT. Changes in NSP upon drug treatments with a q-value < 0.05 and a log2 Fold change (FC) ≥0.38 or ≤-0.38 were further analyzed. Translatome analysis was described in details in the Supplementary Note 2.

Single cell RNA sequencing and data processing
Cryopreserved serial samples from AML patients enrolled in the QUIZOM trial were thawed and subjected to encapsulation and library preparation immediately with ChromiumTM Single Cell 5' v2 Reagent Kit. Paired-end 151 bp reads were generated by illumina NovaSeq 6000. Cell Ranger (version 6.0.0) was applied for quantification.57 Seurat was then used for downstream analysis.58 Cells with fewer than 200 detectable genes or with more than 15% counts mapped to mitochondrial genes were removed.59 Data normalization was carried out with SCTransform.60 Data integration was performed using “FindIntegrationAnchors” and “IntegrateData” functions in Seurat. Unsupervised clustering was conducted with Louvain algorithm and serial resolutions from 0.4 to 5.61 The stability of clusters was examined and an optimal resolution was determined by Clustree.62 Marker genes for each cluster were identified and published haematopoietic cell markers were used to annotate 15 major cell types.40,63 Details about single cell analysis were included in the Supplementary Note 2.

Patients and treatment
Relapse/refractory FLT3-ITD AML patients ≥18 years old and newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD AML patients ≥65 years old unfit for conventional chemotherapy were recruited into a phase II single-arm open-labelled study (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03135054) with informed consent and approval from Institutional Review Board of the University of Hong Kong/Hospital Authority Hong Kong West Cluster (Ref no.: UW 17-099 and UW 05-183 T/846). Among the 45 patients recruited, one patient died before treatment and 4 patients subsequently withdrew from trial based on discretion of treating physicians.

Treatment comprised quizartinib 30 mg daily p.o. and OM at 2 mg daily i.v. for 7 days (1st cycle) or 5 days (subsequent cycles) for every 21-28 days until HSCT or disease progression. Patients achieving complete remission (CR) or complete remission with incomplete haematologic recovery (CRi) were referred for HSCT. Quizartinib was given as post-HSCT maintenance for at least 24 months after engraftment at doses ranging from 30 mg once per day twice weekly to 30 mg daily depending on tolerability.

Primary endpoint was composite complete remission (CRc) defined by CR or CRi according to ELN guideline 2022.2 Secondary endpoints were the percentage of patients who were bridged to HSCT, leukaemia-free (LFS) and overall survivals (OS) (Details refer to the Study Protocol).

Untargeted metabolomics analyses
Around 150 samples comprising FLT3-ITD cells under different combinations of QUIZOM treatments, as well as primary FLT3-ITD AML enriched with LSC, i.e. the triple positive (TP) cells or unselected AML cells in bulk, underwent untargeted metabolomics profiling by liquid chromatography-high resolution mass spectrometry. The untargeted metabolomics procedures was described in detail in the Supplementary Note 2.

Statistical analysis
Categorical variables were compared using Chi-square test and logistic regression whereas continuous variables were compared using t-test, Mann-Whitney U test and Wilcoxon signed rank test. Survival analysis was performed by Kaplan-Meier estimator. LFS and OS were visualised by Kaplan-Meier curves and described by median survival time. Statistical comparisons between two populations were performed by log-rank test. The impacts of various clinical factors on disease outcome were analyzed by univariate analysis using Cox regression.

Experimental data were presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM) from at least three independent experiments. Mouse survival after AML cell line engraftment was evaluated by Kaplan-Meier analysis. All statistical tests were carried out using GraphPad Prism 8.0 or R. p-values were shown in all figures. reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors present a compelling study and were responsive to the previous reviews. My only comment is with respect to their response to Reviewer 1 Comment 1. In the Supplementary Materials the authors state on lines 156-160, "The resulting p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method4 to account for multiple testing. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed based on the fold change of gene effect score produced by limma. The normalized enrichment score (NES) and -log10(adjusted p-value) from GSEA were visualized as volcano plot in Figure 1A." and on lines 357-358, "For the GO terms, multiple testing was controlled using the false discovery rate 357 (FDR) approach, with an adjusted p-value, i.e. q-value < 0.05 to consider significance." Lines 396-397, "Adjusted p-396 values were obtained using the Benjamini-Hochberg method." lines 403-404, "FDR was 403 set at 0.05 and adjusted p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant." Please remove "adjusted p-value" from all of these sentences. FDRs are not adjusted p-values which has been the source of confusion in the applied literature.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The authors have responded to my criticisms.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The manuscript by Zheng et al. entitled “Combination treatment with quizartinib and omacetaxine mepesuccinate reveals metabolic vulnerabilities and mechanisms of drug resistance in FLT3-ITD AML” presents an in-depth study evaluating the therapeutic effects and resistance mechanisms of the combination therapy QUIZOM (quizartinib and omacetaxine mepesuccinate) in FLT3-ITD acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The study is methodologically sound, and offers a compelling narrative linking mitochondrial dysfunction, proteostasis collapse, and immune activation to therapeutic efficacy, while also identifying a lipid metabolism-dependent leukemic stem cell (LSC) population driving resistance. The authors integrate data from functional genomics, translatomics, untargeted metabolomics, single-cell transcriptomics, and a Phase II clinical trial. They convincingly demonstrate that QUIZOM disrupts mitochondrial proteostasis and activates pro-inflammatory signaling, with therapeutic efficacy and immune modulation in patients. Importantly, a phosphatidylcholine metabolism–driven LSC population is implicated in QUIZOM resistance.

The manuscript is comprehensive and impactful. The authors have also provided thoughtful and detailed responses to previous reviewer comments. However, several new scientific points and clarifications are necessary to fully support the claims and broaden the manuscript’s translational relevance.

Major Comments
1. Can phosphatidylcholine (PC) supplementation induce QUIZOM resistance in AML?
The manuscript identifies PLD1-mediated PC metabolism as a key pathway associated with QUIZOM resistance. However, it remains unclear whether supplementation with phosphatidylcholine itself is sufficient to induce resistance in AML cell lines, mirroring the effect of PLD1 overexpression.
Recommendation: Authors should test or at least discuss the potentials of exogenous PC for its effect on QUIZOM sensitivity and whether it recapitulates the protective effect seen with PLD1 overexpression (e.g., Figure 6S). This would help establish the functional significance of PC metabolism in resistance.
2. Does PC supplementation reduce protein aggregate formation after QUIZOM treatment?
The authors show that PLD1 and HSP70 expression reduce protein aggregates in resistant cells. However, it is unknown whether PC supplementation itself could mitigate proteotoxic stress induced by QUIZOM.
Recommendation: If such data exist, they should be presented. Otherwise, the authors should speculate on this mechanism as part of the discussion that link lipid metabolism to proteostasis.
3. Does QUIZOM regulate PLD1 expression directly?
The manuscript suggests PLD1 expression is a feature of the resistant LSC phenotype, but it remains unclear whether PLD1 levels are modulated by QUIZOM treatment in parental or bulk AML populations.
Recommendation: Please clarify whether QUIZOM increases or suppresses PLD1 expression. Clarify whether QUIZOM treatment induces or suppresses PLD1 expression in bulk or triple positive (TP) AML populations.
4. Is PLD1 upregulation at relapse associated with additional somatic mutations?
The study highlights PLD1 as a resistance marker, but does not clearly address whether its upregulation is associated with clonal evolution at relapse.
Recommendation: Please evaluate whether PLD1 upregulation correlates with acquisition of additional mutations in relapse samples, or clarify if it reflects transcriptional reprogramming of pre-existing clones.
5. How can the described metabolic remodeling on immune microenvironment be potentially harnessed for rational treatment design?
The authors provide compelling evidence for cGAS-STING activation and CD8+ T cell responses in clinical responders. However, the broader implications of metabolic remodeling on the immune microenvironment deserve further discussion.
Recommendation: The authors should expand their discussion on the role of tumor metabolism in shaping immune responses, including how mitochondrial collapse, SASP cytokines, and lipid metabolism may influence anti-leukemic immunity. This would help contextualize the clinical significance of QUIZOM-induced immune modulation and provide rationale for combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors or metabolic adjuvants.
6. Did QUIZOM inhibit glycolysis in addition to mitochondrial respiration?
While the authors show that QUIZOM suppresses mitochondrial function and glucose uptake, it is unclear whether glycolysis is directly inhibited. Given that AML cells can display metabolic plasticity, additional metabolic profiling is warranted. Specifically, extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) via Seahorse assays and/or glucose uptake and lactate production assays would be informative.
Recommendation: Please clarify whether glycolytic activity was evaluated and if QUIZOM also impairs glycolysis. If not, this should be acknowledged as a limitation.

Minor Points
• Explicitly mention the source and composition of the NR and PLD1 inhibitor used in rescue experiments in the Methods.
• While the inclusion of a Phase II trial is commendable, the high CRi vs CR rate and transfusion dependence post-remission (as mentioned in the rebuttal) should be more transparently discussed in the main text.
• A schematic summary of the proposed mechanism of resistance involving PLD1, lipid metabolism, proteostasis, and immune escape could aid reader understanding.

Responses to reviewers' comments:
Reviewer #1:
We are grateful to the reviewer’s comments, which have helped us clarify our data
analyses and presentation. Our responses to these comments were given as follows:
1. Line 140-141: The authors state, “P-value was reported after Benjamini-Hochberg
adjustment to account for multiple testings” is not a correct statement because the FDR is
not an adjusted p-value but a different entity. This should read something like, “To account
for multiple hypothesis testing, the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) method
was applied to the resulting p-values.” It would also be useful if the authors stated at the
end of the sentence what FDR threshold was applied to consider genes as significant.
Thanks for the revision. The manuscript was revised as follows:
Supplementary Method. Page 8, Line 319:
“To account for multiple hypothesis testing, the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR)
method was applied to the resulting p-values. FDR was set at 0.05 and adjusted p-value < 0.05
was considered statistically significant.”
2. Lines 157-158 & 160-162: The authors state, “The expression of mitochondrial genes was
quantified and cells with more than 15% counts mapped to mitochondrial genes were
removed from further analysis.” Then they state, “Datasets were then merged and
normalized using ‘SCTransform’ v2 function in Seurat with regression on mitochondrial
gene percentage.” The authors should clarify what type of regression model was applied
because the percentage is bounded by 0 naturally and then bounded by 15 due to their
filtering, so linear regression would not be appropriate to directly apply. Also, they should
explain why they filtered then modelled mitochondrial gene percentage.
The reviewer pointed out correctly that linear regression model should not apply where
dependent variables were bounded. Therefore, we used a regularized negative binomial
regression model in the normalization step, an approach which has been reported by the
SCTransform.19 In this normalization process, the Unique Molecular Identifier (UMI) was the
dependent variable and the mitochondrial gene percentage was an independent variable
(covariate), thereby potential impact of mitochondrial gene content (0-15%) could be negated
in the normalized expression value of genes in each cell.19,20 Those cells with more than 15%
mitochondrial genes were excluded as they might be unhealthy and unreliable for
downstream analysis.21,22 The 15% cut-off was widely adopted in previous publications.23,24
Therefore, we have revised the text as follows:
Supplementary Methods, Page 9, Line 324:
“A regularized negative binomial regression model was used in the normalization step, an
approach which has been reported by the SCTransform.20 In this normalization process, the
Unique Molecular Identifier (UMI) was the dependent variable and the mitochondrial gene
percentage was an independent variable (covariate), thereby potential impact of
mitochondrial gene content (0-15%) could be negated in the normalized expression value of
genes in each cell.19,20 Those cells with more than 15% mitochondrial genes were excluded as
they might be unhealthy and unreliable for downstream analysis.22,23 The 15% cut-off was
widely adopted in previous publications.24,25
3. Line 162-163: The authors should explain what is meant by “top 3000 integration
features.”
In this study, we have analyzed and integrated the 45 single cell transcriptome datasets
arising from patient samples. First, a subset of 3000 “highly variable genes” were selected
from each dataset based on their standardized variance. They represented mostly genes that
were associated with distinct cell populations or functional states in each dataset and hence
might be more biologically relevant. The “highly variable genes ” that were selected from
multiple datasets will be ranked based on their prevalence. For example, “highly variable
genes” that occurred in all 45 datasets will be ranked the top and others that occurred in only
44 samples will be ranged the second etc. Another 3000 genes at the top ranks based on this
algorithm will be selected. They represented genes that were most relevant and recurrent in
our datasets. This workflow has been described and has become the standard pipeline of
Seurat.26
These points were now incorporated in the revised manuscript as follows:
Supplementary Methods, Page 9, Line 332:
“We have then integrate the 45 single cell transcriptome datasets arising from patient
samples. First, a subset of 3000 “highly variable genes” were selected from each dataset
based on their standardized variance using “FindVariableFeatures” function in Seurat.26 They
represented mostly genes that were associated with distinct cell populations or functional
states in each dataset and hence might be more biologically relevant. The “highly variable
genes ” that were selected from multiple datasets will be ranked based on their prevalence.
For example, “highly variable genes” that occurred in all 45 datasets will be ranked the top
and others that occurred in only 44 samples will be ranged the second etc. Another 3000
genes at the top ranks based on this algorithm will be selected using
“SelectIntegrationFeatures” in Seurat.65”
4. Line 166: Please provide a reference for the Louvain algorithm.
The reference for the Louvain algorithm was provided as follows:
Supplementary Methods, Page 10, Line 390:
“Unsupervised clustering with Louvain algorithm35,36 and resolution=0.4 using Seurat’s
function “FindClusters” were applied to the HSC-MPP population and 7 clusters were
identified.”
5. Line 197: The authors state that a secondary endpoint was “rate of patients bridged to
HSCT.” Because “rate” is used that would more often be interpreted as the time to HSCT
instead of as a binary outcome. Because they reported the frequency and percentage of
patients received HSCT, this sentence should be rephrased.
Points are well taken. The manuscript was revised as follows:
Page 4, Line 134:
“Secondary endpoints were the percentage of patients who were bridged to HSCT, leukaemia-
free (LFS) and overall survivals (OS).”
6. Figure 1A: The authors should indicate in the caption what the plotted points represent
(genes or pathways) and the graph should include a y-axis label.
Thank you for the comment. The figure and the legend have been revised as follows.
Figure 1A
Legend to Figure 1A
“Analysis of genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout data (DepMap) revealed that FLT3-ITD AML
cell lines were more vulnerable to the knockout of genes involved in translation, FLT3
signaling, respiratory electron transport, and DNA repair process (see also Supplementary

7. Results; Figures: MOLM-14 is discussed in the Results section on line 209 but is not
included as a cell line in Supplementary Methods lines 299-303 and MOLM-14 is not
depicted in these figures. Did the authors examine MOLM-14 and get negative results?
MOLM-14 was mentioned in the Results because it was included in the DepMap database.

“MOLM-14, which was included in the DepMap database, was not available in our institute.
However, its sensitivity to therapeutic agents was remarkably similar to those of MOLM-13
and MV4-11.1-3”

QO somewhere so that the tables can stand alone.

small sample size and that the effective sample size in a Cox PH model is the number of
events, and that typically we require ~20 events per variable included in the model, a
multivariate model with 4 variables is not reasonable for this dataset (27 OS events; 22 LFS

“The difference in gene knock-out effect was identified by limma (linear models for microarray

“Survival analysis was performed by Kaplan-Meier estimator. LFS and OS were visualised by

Reviewer #2:
Major criticisms:
What is missing is the tolerability of this regimen- other than the woefully-inadequate
phrase “Treatment was generally tolerated”. Were there early deaths? What were common
adverse events? What was the median time to response? Given that there was a high
overall response rate, but low overall true CR rate, the implication is that these were

cytopenia: One patient died of pneumonia and pulmonary haemorrhage on day 29 from

is 23 days (Range: 17-62 days).

marrow aplasia. In fact, 22 out of 27 (81%) patients with CRi, and overall 22 out of 33 (67%)

relapse or alloHSCT.

Reviewer #3:
Evaluating the combination of HHT/omacetaxine and quizartinib is certainly reasonable
enough, but this reviewer was hoping to find within this manuscript a new and exciting
message suitable for the readers of Nature Cancer.
We thank the reviewer for this comment. In this manuscript, we adopted a staged and
unbiased approach to identify the vulnerabilities of FLT3-ITD AML pertinent to protein
translation and reported the hitherto undescribed therapeutic mechanisms based on
perturbed metabolism and proteostasis. To prove the principle, we initiated a Phase II
clinical trial and demonstrated, in a cohort including heavily pre-treated patients, high
remission rate and long-term survival over 70% among HSCT recipients. Using serially
collected samples, we demonstrated for the first time the mechanistic link of metabolic
remodelling and immune activation in clinical responders to perturbed proteostasis and the
mechanism of drug resistance with particular reference to PLD1/JNK/HSPA1B activation in a
primitive leukaemia population. These findings were summarized in the graphical abstract.
We believed that these information will bring important insights to both leukaemia biologists
and clinical haematologists and will provide a solid and mechanistic foundation based on
which future clinical trials can be designed.
To strengthen the manuscript for the readers of Nature Cancer, we have performed a series
of new experiments to highlight the following novel concepts with respects to therapeutic
developments in FLT3-ITD AML:
1. FLT3-ITD AML is vulnerable to perturbation of mitochondria-assisted protein refolding via
suppression of HSP70 signaling (Figure 2E-2T, Extended Data Fig. 2J-2R, Figure 3 and Extended
Data Fig. 3);
2. Perturbation of mitochondria by QUIZOM in FLT3-ITD AML resulted in pro-inflammatory
signals and cGAS-STING activation (Figure 4, Extended Data Fig. 4, Figure 5H-5N);
3. Drug resistance in FLT3-ITD AML was mediated by persistence and emergence of resistant
clones manifesting LSC signature with enhanced chaperone protein refolding activity and
specific metabolic dependence. These phenotypes were mitigated by c-Fos/c-Jun and PLD1
inhibition, thereby overcoming drug resistance (Figure 3G, 3J, 3L-3N, Figure 6J-6W, Extended
Data Fig. 6J-6K) .
Details of these experiments and the results have been incorporated in the revised
manuscript and our responses were listed in the relevant points that followed.
Perhaps most importantly the clinical data do not convince that this combination has great
future potential. Quizartinib monotherapy in relapsed/refractory patients (two cohorts –
one aged >60 and another aged >18 relapsed after salvage or HSCT) gave CR rates of ~46-
56% with median LFS of around 3 months and median OS of 6 months (as per PMID
29859851). This compares with ~3.5months LFS and 9.5 months OS in the current study
which features arguably a more favourable patient population (e.g. median age here is 57.5
versus median age of 69 in cohort 1 of the Lancet Oncology paper). Thus the leukaemia free
survival with QUIZOM here in patients who did not receive transplant was indistinguishable
from historic data for quizartinib monotherapy.
Points very well taken. The phase II clinical trial in the current study (QUIZOM) was intended
to test the concept and therapeutic efficacy of combining a FLT3 inhibitor and a protein
translation inhibitor. Importantly, the clinical samples have helped us examine the
therapeutic mechanisms and identify potential targets of drug resistance.
In general, we find it difficult to compare outcome between clinical trials as the drug dose,
regimen and patient characteristics were different. Of note, the doses of quizartinib used
were also different. In the Lancet Oncology paper, the first cohort of patients was treated
with 200 mg daily dose continuously, and subsequent cohorts received reducing doses to 135
mg, 90 mg and 60 mg daily. In QUIZOM cohort, patients were treated with 30 mg daily
quizartinib continuously and simultaneously with omacetaxine mepesuccinate.
However, in response to the reviewer’s comments, we have tabulated the characteristics and
treatment outcome of the relapse/refractory patients treated with single agent quizartinib
from the Lancet Oncology paper by Cortes et al published in 201835 and data from QUIZOM
focusing on relapse/refractory (R/R) patients as follows:

with metabolic remodelling and perturbed proteostasis via the activation of

The authors have responded to my criticisms.

Reviewer #4:
The manuscript by Zheng et al. entitled “Combination treatment with quizartinib and
omacetaxine mepesuccinate reveals metabolic vulnerabilities and mechanisms of drug resistance
in FLT3-ITD AML” presents an in-depth study evaluating the therapeutic effects and resistance
mechanisms of the combination therapy QUIZOM (quizartinib and omacetaxine mepesuccinate)
in FLT3-ITD acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The study is methodologically sound, and offers a
compelling narrative linking mitochondrial dysfunction, proteostasis collapse, and immune
activation to therapeutic efficacy, while also identifying a lipid metabolism-dependent leukemic
stem cell (LSC) population driving resistance. The authors integrate data from functional
genomics, translatomics, untargeted metabolomics, single-cell transcriptomics, and a Phase II
clinical trial. They convincingly demonstrate that QUIZOM disrupts mitochondrial proteostasis
and activates pro-inflammatory signaling, with therapeutic efficacy and immune modulation in
patients. Importantly, a phosphatidylcholine metabolism–driven LSC population is implicated in
QUIZOM resistance.
The manuscript is comprehensive and impactful. The authors have also provided thoughtful and
detailed responses to previous reviewer comments. However, several new scientific points and
clarifications are necessary to fully support the claims and broaden the manuscript’s translational
relevance.
Major Comments
1. Can phosphatidylcholine (PC) supplementation induce QUIZOM resistance in AML?
The manuscript identifies PLD1-mediated PC metabolism as a key pathway associated with
QUIZOM resistance. However, it remains unclear whether supplementation with
phosphatidylcholine itself is sufficient to induce resistance in AML cell lines, mirroring the effect
of PLD1 overexpression.
Recommendation: Authors should test or at least discuss the potentials of exogenous PC for its
effect on QUIZOM sensitivity and whether it recapitulates the protective effect seen with PLD1
overexpression (e.g., Figure 6S). This would help establish the functional significance of PC
metabolism in resistance.
We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestion. We have since then examined the effect of
phosphatidylcholine supplement and found that it significantly reduced QUIZOM-mediated growth
suppression and apoptosis induction (Extended Data Fig. 6J and 6K). These new observations further
strengthened our proposition in the initial submission that activation of PLD1-governed PC
metabolism can confer QUIZOM resistance in AML.
The manuscript has been revised as follows:
Results, Page 11, Line 413
“Supplementation of phosphatidylcholine (PC), the substrate of PLD1, also induced QUIZOM resistance
in AML (Extended Data Fig. 6J and 6K)”
Extended Data Fig. 6J
Extended Data Fig. 6K

apoptosis induction by QUIZOM (2nM quizartinib and 5nM OM) in MV4-11 and MOLM-13 cell lines (Paired
t test, SEM shown as error bar, n=3).”

The authors show that PLD1 and HSP70 expression reduce protein aggregates in resistant cells.
However, it is unknown whether PC supplementation itself could mitigate proteotoxic stress
induced by QUIZOM.

The manuscript suggests PLD1 expression is a feature of the resistant LSC phenotype, but it

4. Is PLD1 upregulation at relapse associated with additional somatic mutations?
The study highlights PLD1 as a resistance marker, but does not clearly address whether its
upregulation is associated with clonal evolution at relapse.
Recommendation: Please evaluate whether PLD1 upregulation correlates with acquisition of

We have examined the somatic mutations at relapse. However, there was no significant change in

“However, there was no significant change in the top 10 common mutations in the cohort between

5. How can the described metabolic remodeling on immune microenvironment be potentially

The authors provide compelling evidence for cGAS-STING activation and CD8+ T cell responses in
clinical responders. However, the broader implications of metabolic remodeling on the immune
microenvironment deserve further discussion.
Recommendation: The authors should expand their discussion on the role of tumor metabolism

6. Did QUIZOM inhibit glycolysis in addition to mitochondrial respiration?
While the authors show that QUIZOM suppresses mitochondrial function and glucose uptake, it

treatment in MV4-11 and MOLM-13.
(N) QUIZOM reduced both basal and maximum ECAR in MV4-11 and MOLM-13 (Paired t test,
SEM shown as error bar, n=3).”

• Explicitly mention the source and composition of the NR and PLD1 inhibitor used in rescue
